home_eyebrow: Open research on modern board games
home_q: What does an AI learn when it plays a board game tens of thousands of times against itself?
home_lede: We let AI agents learn modern board games only by playing against copies of themselves — nobody teaches them a strategy. Then each AI plays thousands of games, and we compare what the winners did differently: which cards, combinations and habits go with winning.
step1: It plays against copies of itself and keeps what wins. Over tens of thousands of games (millions of moves) it becomes a strong player — or, if it does not pass its strength test, we say so.
step2: The AI then plays 2,000 more games. Each deal has a number, so anyone can replay exactly the same games.
step3: At the end of every game each player's points are counted card by card. Comparing winners with losers shows what goes with winning.
games_sub: Open a game to see its discoveries, the strategy in plain words, every card and how the AI was trained.
models_finished: AIs that passed the strength test
model_legacy: Not finished: did not pass the strength test
add_text: Anyone can add a game. A coding agent (Claude Code, Codex and others) follows the repository's step-by-step guides: it writes the rules in its own words, builds the card data, the rules engine and its tests, trains the AI and runs the standard experiments.
add_1: Open a branch and say which game you want, e.g. "add the game Azul".
add_2: The agent works through the guides; every step leaves files you can check.
add_3: Automatic checks, a test for every rule and card, and a second review must pass before training.
add_4: Open a pull request; the site updates when it is merged.
trust_h: Why you can trust the numbers
trust_1: Every rule of the game is written down and tested; rules and cards are checked against at least two independent sources.
trust_2: Every set of games can be replayed: the same AI and the same numbered deals give exactly the same games, and an automatic check replays some of them after every change.
trust_3: Every AI must pass a strength test before we call it finished. An AI that did not pass is marked "early" and its findings "tentative" wherever they appear.
trust_4: Small samples are greyed out and every effect shows how uncertain it is.
caveat: These are patterns in the AI's own games: they show what winners have more of, not always why. The AI plays well against an equally strong copy of itself — that is not a proven best strategy.

how_lede: Every number on this site comes from thousands of games an AI played against copies of itself. Here is what the measures mean and how far you can trust them.
how_example: "{item}: effect on winning {lift}" means: in the AI's {game} games with {players}, players who had {item} {T:in_own_board} won {win} of their games, against {base} for the average player: {lift2} more, shown rounded as {lift}. (The average is a little above {even} because a tie counts as a win for both.) It does not prove that {item} causes the win — maybe winners simply had time to play it — but a big, steady difference over thousands of games is a strong hint.
g_lift_d: How much more (or less) often players win when they have this card, type or habit, compared with the average player, in percentage points. 0 = no difference. It shows what goes with winning, not what causes it.
g_pp_d: The difference between two percentages: from 50 % to 58 % is +8 percentage points.
g_err: ± and the line through a bar
g_err_d: The uncertainty. The range is 2 "standard errors" either side of the value: the true value lies inside it about 95 % of the time. More games give a narrower range.
g_unclear_d: The uncertainty range crosses 0: the card or type may have no effect at all. Do not build a plan on it.
g_edge_d: How many more copies of a card the winner had than the loser of the same game, on average. It compares players of the same game, so luck of the deal and game length cancel out.
g_presence_d: In what share of final forests (or player boards) the card appears at least once.
g_points_d: Average points one copy of the card scored at the end, counted only where it was played.
g_points_board_d: Average points a card brings to a forest, over all forests, also those without it (they count as 0). A common card ranks higher here than in "points per copy".
g_type_d: A simple label for a player's whole board, e.g. the tree symbol or habitat it has most of. It shows which overall plans win.
g_turns_d: How many turns each player had in a game: the total number of turns divided by the number of players. A game can end in the middle of a round, so the raw number can have a half; we round it.
g_mirror_d: Every seat is played by the same AI, so everyone plays equally well; the differences come from choices and luck, not from a weaker opponent.
g_strength_d: Before we call an AI finished it must clearly beat opponents it never trained against and a simple greedy player. Only a finished AI is strong enough that its games mean something.
g_early_d: An AI that has not passed the strength test. Its findings are shown with a warning: treat them as a first hint, not advice.
g_greedy_d: A fixed program that does not learn: it always takes the move that scores the most points right now. A good AI must beat it almost every time.
g_paired_d: The same deal is played twice with the players swapping seats, so luck of the cards cancels out.
g_steps_d: One step is one decision the AI practised while learning. Millions of steps make tens of thousands of training games.
g_grey_d: Cards or groups that appeared too rarely for their numbers to be trusted.
g_corr_d: The site shows what winners have more of. Whether that is why they won is a judgement — the written notes try to make it, carefully. "Players with X win more often" never means "X makes you win".
g_explains_d: If you knew only that one thing (e.g. how many cards were left in the deck at the end), you could predict about 74.5 % of the ups and downs in game length. Two causes can overlap, so their shares do not add up.
g_seed_d: Each game is dealt from a numbered shuffle. With the same AI and the same numbers anyone can replay exactly the same games — that is how the numbers can be checked.
